cultivar: Varies; Okumidori in at least one named lot
processing: Shaded leaf is steamed and dried flat into tencha, then ground in stone mills into powder, as is standard for fine matcha.
harvest_season: Spring. Better lots are described as hand-picked first flush.
appearance_dry: Fine, bright to deep green powder.
appearance_liquor: Opaque green, thick with fine foam when whisked.
appearance_wet: No spent leaf: the powder is drunk whole.
taste_profile: Like other shaded Yame teas, it leans to umami and soft sweetness, with little astringency; specific notes depend on the farm and cultivar.

brewing.notes: Sift first, use water well below the boil and whisk until smooth. Use more powder and less water for a thick koicha only with a grade sold for it.

vintage_note: Sold fresh by grade and harvest year, sometimes naming the farmer and cultivar. Buy recent milling in small tins, because the colour and aroma fade quickly once open. It has no formal appellation of its own, so the words on the tin depend on the seller.
description:
Hoshino matcha is stone-ground powder from the tea village of Hoshino in Yame, Fukuoka. It is a place description rather than a protected name, and the village is better known for gyokuro than for matcha. Its shaded-tea skills carry over naturally.

The leaf is covered before picking, as gyokuro is, then made into tencha and milled.

A good bowl has a smooth, savoury sweetness. Prepare it as any matcha: sift, keep the water off the boil and whisk with a quick wrist motion. The character varies a lot by maker, and single-cultivar Okumidori lots are one example on the market.

Look for the producer, the cultivar and the harvest year. A vague 'Hoshino' on a cheap bag says little.
history:
Tencha is the newer half of Hoshino's tea story. Hoshino Seichaen, a family firm founded in 1946, built its name on traditional gyokuro and is credited with completing the first full-scale tencha facility in Kyushu in 1989.

Small farms also make tencha alongside gyokuro, among them Kurazumi, whose awards are mainly in gyokuro. Little else is documented about how matcha developed in the village.
